title: A design partner versus a vendor
metaTitle: Design partner or vendor, decide first
excerpt: A partner shares the decision. A vendor receives a specification. Name which relationship you are offering before the proposal, or the project will fight itself.
alt: Three hands holding coffee cups together over a wooden table, two with latte art, a shared table for an article about choosing a partner or a vendor.
caption: Cups on one table, before the roles are confused. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a design partner and a vendor?
faqs.answer: A partner shares the decision about what to build and what to leave out, and is accountable for a result a stranger can use. A vendor receives a specification and delivers against it. Both can be honest. The project fights itself when one side expects a shared decision and the other expects a ticket.

faqs.question: When is a vendor relationship the right one?
faqs.answer: Choose a vendor when the work is defined, the acceptance criteria are real, and you want execution more than judgment. A fixed set of pages, or a screen that already has a signed flow, can fit. If the brief is still a feeling, a vendor contract will turn every discovery into a change request.

faqs.question: Can one studio be both?
faqs.answer: Yes, on different phases, if you name the switch. Discovery and a first version can be a partnership, and a later batch of specified pages can be delivery against a list. Write that switch down, or the invoice and the feedback will assume different relationships in the same week.

markdown:
A design partner vs vendor choice should be named before anyone writes a proposal. A partner shares the decision about what to make and what to refuse. A vendor receives a specification and delivers it. If you do not say which relationship you are offering, the project will fight itself in the first round of feedback.

The fight is ordinary and expensive. One side brings a problem. The other was hired to receive an answer. Both feel misled, and both are partly right, because the role was never written down.

## What each role is for

A partner is in the room while the problem is still soft. They help decide the audience, the job of the page, the slice of product that should exist first, and the things you will not build. They are accountable for a result a stranger can use, not only for a file that matches a request. When the founder is wrong about the sentence, a partner says so while changing it is still cheap.

A vendor is the right shape when the decision is already made. Here are the pages. Here is the content. Here is the acceptance test. The craft is execution: type, code, a launch that matches the spec. Asking a vendor to invent the company inside a fixed list of screens is how the list explodes and the tone turns sour.

Hanabi's public stance, clarity over complexity, fits a partner role. The studio designs and builds, and the judgment is part of the work. That is not the only honorable stance. A team with a finished design, who wants production, should be able to buy production. The mistake is a brochure that says partner and a contract that says deliver these comps.

You can hear the difference in the questions. A partner asks what the visitor must understand, and what you will not do. A vendor asks for the files, the kit, and the date. Both questions are professional. They belong to different jobs. If you want both, you are looking at two phases, and the phases should have names.

## Where an unnamed role breaks

Feedback is the usual break. A founder writes "make it pop" and also "you are the expert, do what you think." Those are two relationships in one comment. The first is a vendor instruction, vague but directional. The second is a partner invitation. A studio that accepts both will guess, and the guess will be called a miss.

Scope is the next break. In a partnership, discovering that the product needs an empty state and an error, not only a hero, is the work. In a vendor engagement, those screens are new line items if they were not in the spec. Neither rule is cruel. Applying the wrong rule is what makes the invoice feel like a betrayal.

Access is the third break. A partner needs real content, a staging link, and a founder who can decide. A vendor can sometimes work from a pack. If you hired a partner and then disappeared, the partner is blocked. If you hired a vendor and then filled their week with strategy meetings, you are spending execution time on a role you did not buy.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks a public page to make its purpose clear. The same test belongs on a services page and in the first call. If a stranger cannot tell whether you share decisions or receive specs, the buyers who arrive will bring both hopes. You will spend kickoff sorting them, which is late.

## Say it in public, and on the call

Write one paragraph the site can keep. "We help decide the offer, then design and build. We are a poor fit if the screens are already final and you want production only." Or the other paragraph, if that is the truth. Studios that truly do both should say which engagements start where. Ambiguity feels polite. It costs a month.

On the intro call, ask which role they want, in those words, and repeat it back. "You want a partner through launch, and you do not have a sitemap." Or "The pages are approved and you want them built." If they say a bit of both, name the phase that is still a decision and the phase that is a spec. Do not smile past the knot.

The portfolio should agree with the paragraph. A partner's case note records a decision: what the page was for, what was refused. A vendor's note can be proud of craft without pretending a strategy week that did not happen. Down the Cove, an ecommerce migration and redesign, is work where decision and build are tangled. Show the tangle if you sell it. Show a clean build if that is the offer.

Price follows the role. A partner's fee includes time for a wrong idea to be found and replaced. A vendor's fee includes time to match a spec. Selling partner behavior at a vendor price is how studios resent the work and founders resent the bill. Name the role, then the number. Do not let the number secretly choose the role.

## How the week feels after you choose

A partnership week contains a decision. The review ends with a sentence everyone can repeat, written down. The founder brings the constraint from the business. The studio brings the constraint from the page, the type, and what the user will actually do. Disagreement is part of the service. A studio that only agrees is a vendor with better manners.

A vendor week checks the spec. Did the page match. Do the states you listed exist. Are the bugs the agreed bugs. New ideas go to a list with a cost, or they wait. This can feel strict to someone who wanted a collaborator. It feels fair to someone who wanted the list built by Friday. Fairness was the reason to choose.

The behavior has to match the label. A partner can say a headline will not survive a stranger, and offer another. A vendor who rewrites an approved headline without asking has left the role. A partner who will not recommend, and only asks for more adjectives, has ducked the role. The week is the contract, more than the word on the cover.

Tools follow. A partner may use Figma while structure is cheap to change, then the browser, with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, when real words and motion decide. A vendor building from finished files should still leave the repository with the client. The role changes who decides. It should not change whether the client can keep the work.

## What each side owes

If you hire a partner, you owe decisions. One person who can say yes. The truth about the offer, including the messy parts. Feedback that separates "this fails the job" from "I prefer blue." Time in the week of the review, not a silent fortnight and a surprise.

If you hire a vendor, you owe a spec that is finished enough to build. Content, or a date it will arrive. A kit they may use. One list of acceptance criteria. A new audience halfway through is a new project. Call it that, so the date is allowed to move in public.

If you are the studio, owe the mirror. Do not take a partner fee and hide behind "tell us what you want." Do not take a vendor fee and relitigate the strategy in every review because the work feels small. The role is a promise about where judgment lives. Keep the promise in ordinary weeks, which is when it usually slips.

Write the rules in a short note. Who decides. How feedback arrives. What is out of scope. Where files live. On a Hanabi project the client portal holds brand files, docs, and updates so the decision is not only a chat. The tool can vary. The written role cannot.

## Switching, or refusing to

Some projects should start as a partnership and become a build. Mark the meeting. "These pages are now the spec. A new page is a change." Both sides relax, because the rules changed where everyone could see them.

Some projects should never become a partnership. The founder has a team and a clear kit, and they want production. Pretending to be strategic so the sale sounds larger will insult that team by week two. Sell the build. Leave the repository in their name.

Some founders need a partner and ask for a vendor price because that is the shape they know. Say what the smaller price buys. A shorter partnership, one surface, can be real. A full partnership at a vendor price is a story the margin will regret.

The proposal is where the choice becomes a document a stranger can read. [What a proposal should contain](/blog/what-a-proposal-should-contain) names the pages or the slice, the exclusions, the ownership, and the way you will talk. Read it before you send a PDF that says partner in the title and assets in the body.

If you want to see work where a decision and a build are both visible, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful question is whether you need a studio inside the decision, or a studio that will carry a decision you have already made.
